newsitem.title: INDIA: India communists to go if Congress joins coalition.
newsitem.headline: India communists to go if Congress joins coalition.

text.p: India's main communist parties will quit Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's alliance if the Congress party, giving him vital support in parliament, joins the government, communist officials said on Thursday.
"In the unlikely event of the Congress joining the government, we won't be staying on," an official of the Communist Party of India (CPI) told Reuters.
He said the CPI National Council will meet on January 4, a day after Congress is due to elect a new leader to head the party in parliament, to review the emerging scenario.
"At the moment all the talk of Congress joining the government is hypothetical," the official said.

Speculation has mounted recently over the Congress' attitude to Deve Gowda after India's oldest political machine was plunged into a crisis with the forced resignation of former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao as its president.
Rao had promised to support Deve Gowda's coalition when it took power on June 1, to fend off a challenge from the main opposition Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

But his successor Sitaram Kesri has frequently threatened to review his party's ties with the 13-party United Front alliance, mainly over their differences on who should rule the most populous state of Uttar Pradesh.
Congress has failed to win Deve Gowda's support for the Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP) of erstwhile Hindu untouchables to lead a coalition to run the state government.
Uttar Pradesh has been under federal rule from New Delhi since inconclusive local elections in September.

The Congress has 142 deputies in the 545-member lower house while the communists control some 60 seats. But there are other regional groups in Deve Gowda's coalition that consider any proximity to Congress as suicidal for their domestic power bases because Congress is the main local rival.
It was not immediately clear what the attitude of these other groups would be to a power-sharing arrangement with the Congress.
Deve Gowda's own Janata Dal party has 46 deputies, which with the Congress' 142, does not add up to a majority in the 545-member house. The BJP and its allies have 195 deputies.
Analysts say the BJP, which needs to consolidate a power base in Uttar Pradesh, this week decided to back the BSP, leaving the United Front and Congress out of the picture.
Yet some Congress stalwarts, led by former ministers Rajesh Pilot and Sharad Pawar, say they are not averse to joining Deve Gowda's government.
The two are the key rivals to Kesri in the leadership contest for the Congress Parliamentary Party.
Kesri is widely regarded as close to some of Deve Gowda's socialist allies.

"There are people in the government who would prefer an alliance with the Congress to keep the left out," one official of the Communist Party of India-Marxist (CPI-M), the main communist group, told Reuters.
"But as we see it there won't be much support for the government if such a move does take place," the official said.
The Congress has its own compulsions to support the government, communist leaders say.
"It doesn't want a mid-term poll and it doesn't want to take chances against the BJP," one CPI official said.
